triage.reason: Infant with asymmetric thigh folds or a positive Ortolani/Barlow maneuver; diagnosed by exam and ultrasound, a core pediatric screening topic.

demographics: Left hip affected more often than right
More common in Native American populations; less common in African American populations

risk_factors.text: Family history of developmental dysplasia of the hip
Tight swaddling with hips extended and adducted

family_history: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in a parent or sibling
exposures: Tight swaddling with legs extended and pressed together

chief_complaints.text: Her hip clicks when I change her diaper
One thigh crease is higher than the other
One leg looks shorter than the other

hpi.onset: At birth or first detected at newborn exam
hpi.duration: Present since birth; may be noticed over first weeks to months
hpi.progression: Hip is unstable and can become dislocated over weeks if not treated; findings may appear or worsen during growth
hpi.location: Usually one hip, left more often than right; bilateral in about 20%
hpi.quality: No pain in infants; may feel a clunk
hpi.timing: Noticed during diaper changes or well-child visits

associated_symptoms.text: A click or clunk when the hip is moved
One leg appears shorter than the other
Less movement when spreading the legs

pertinent_negatives: Irritability or refusal to move the leg
Swelling or erythema of the hip
Neurologic signs such as abnormal tone or asymmetric reflexes

positives.text: Less ability to spread legs fully

atypical.how_it_differs: Older walking children present with a painless limp, waddling gait, leg length discrepancy, or lordosis rather than a click or unstable hip on exam.
Bilateral hip dysplasia can be symmetric, so there may be no leg length discrepancy or asymmetric folds; limited abduction and waddling gait once walking are clues.

general.severe: Well-appearing infant; may have an asymmetric posture with the affected leg slightly shorter and externally rotated
general.critical: Older infant or child with a limp or waddling gait, not acutely ill

findings.maneuver: With the infant supine and hips flexed to 90 degrees, abduct the hips and gently lift the greater trochanter forward.
findings.finding: A palpable clunk as the femoral head reduces into the acetabulum.

findings.maneuver: With the infant supine, flex the hip to 90 degrees and adduct the thigh while applying gentle posterior pressure.
findings.finding: The femoral head slips out of the acetabulum, indicating an unstable but not yet dislocated hip.

findings.maneuver: With the infant supine and hips flexed to 90 degrees, gently abduct both hips.
findings.finding: Reduced passive abduction, usually less than 60 degrees on the affected side.

findings.maneuver: Inspect the infant's thighs and buttocks with legs extended and together.
findings.finding: Asymmetric skin folds, with an extra fold or a higher crease on the affected side.

findings.maneuver: With the infant supine and hips flexed to 90 degrees, compare the height of the knees.
findings.finding: One knee is lower than the other, suggesting a dislocated hip on the lower side.
No tenderness with gentle palpation or movement.

findings.maneuver: Assess muscle tone and deep tendon reflexes, especially in the lower extremities.

findings.finding: No swelling or erythema of the hip.

imaging.preferred_when: Infants younger than 4-6 months, before femoral head ossification

findings.text: Alpha angle less than 60 degrees indicating a shallow acetabulum
Femoral head dislocated or subluxated at rest or with stress (dynamic instability)
Beta angle greater than 55 degrees indicating a steep cartilaginous roof

imaging.preferred_when: Infants older than 4-6 months and children, after femoral head ossification

findings.text: Femoral head superior and lateral to Perkins line (dislocated)
Delayed or asymmetric ossification of the femoral head

initial.why: First-line imaging for infants younger than 4-6 months; assesses acetabular morphology and dynamic hip stability
initial.only_if: infant younger than 4-6 months or before femoral head ossification

initial.why: First-line imaging for older infants and children once the femoral head is ossified

not_indicated.why: No role in routine screening or diagnosis; may be used for surgical planning or complicated cases
Unnecessary radiation exposure; no role in routine evaluation
No systemic illness or inflammation expected; normal and non-diagnostic
Not indicated; no infection or inflammation

decision_points: Ultrasound is the imaging study of choice in infants younger than 4-6 months; AP pelvis radiograph is used after femoral head ossification.
All infants with a positive Ortolani or Barlow maneuver, or with significant risk factors, should have hip ultrasound by 4-6 weeks of age.
Refer to pediatric orthopedics if ultrasound or radiograph shows dysplasia, subluxation, or dislocation.
Do not order a lab workup for isolated hip dysplasia unless another diagnosis is suspected.

differential.name: Septic arthritis of the hip
differential.why_considered: Infant or young child with a painful hip, limp, pseudoparalysis, fever, or refusal to move the leg may have a hip that appears asymmetric or dysplastic on exam.
differential.trigger: Fever, pain, or refusal to move the leg

history: Irritability or crying with diaper changes
exam: Hip held flexed, abducted, and externally rotated
Pain with any passive hip motion
Swelling or erythema over the hip
labs: Positive blood culture or joint aspirate
imaging: MRI shows joint effusion and synovitis

differential.name: Transient synovitis
differential.why_considered: Common cause of an acute limp and hip pain in a young child; may be confused with DDH in an older child, but transient synovitis is painful and self-limited.

history: Recent viral upper respiratory infection within 1-2 weeks
Acute onset limp or refusal to bear weight
Pain varies, often worse in the morning
exam: Painful restricted hip motion, especially abduction and internal rotation
No orthopedic instability; hip remains located
Well-appearing or mildly ill, no sepsis
labs: Typically normal WBC, ESR, CRP or only mildly elevated
imaging: Ultrasound may show a small hip effusion
No acetabular dysplasia or dislocation on x-ray or ultrasound

differential.name: Proximal femoral focal deficiency
differential.why_considered: Congenital leg length discrepancy with a short thigh may look like a dislocated hip on Galeazzi sign.

history: Visible shortening of one thigh noted at birth
exam: Marked leg length discrepancy with short thigh segment
imaging: Radiograph shows absent or short proximal femur with normal acetabulum
Ultrasound shows no normal femoral head position

differential.name: Congenital coxa vara
differential.why_considered: Painless limp and leg length discrepancy in a young child; needs hip imaging to distinguish from DDH.

history: Painless limp noticed when child starts walking
imaging: Radiograph shows reduced femoral neck-shaft angle, typically less than 110 degrees
Femoral head remains in acetabulum; no dislocation

differential.name: Benign neonatal hip click
differential.why_considered: A soft click on newborn exam may raise concern for DDH, but most clicks are not associated with true instability.

exam: A click without a clunk on Ortolani or Barlow maneuver

severity.mild: Acetabular dysplasia without instability: the femoral head is located but the acetabulum is shallow on ultrasound. Exam may be normal or show only a soft click. Many stabilize spontaneously by 4-6 weeks; some are treated with abduction bracing.
severity.moderate: Unstable but reducible hip: the hip is in the socket at rest but can be dislocated with a Barlow maneuver and reduced with abduction or an Ortolani maneuver. There may be asymmetric folds or laxity, but the joint remains subluxatable rather than fixed.
severity.severe: Dislocated hip: the femoral head lies outside the acetabulum at rest. It may be reducible early with an Ortolani maneuver or irreducible later, with limited abduction, a Galeazzi sign, and leg length discrepancy. Typically needs orthopedic referral and often closed or open reduction with spica casting.

red_flags.finding: Fever, pain, irritability, and refusal to move the leg
red_flags.meaning: Septic arthritis of the hip until excluded; urgent aspiration and orthopedic evaluation.

red_flags.finding: Diffuse tenderness, erythema, or swelling over the hip
red_flags.meaning: Infection or inflammation, not isolated DDH; do not delay workup.

red_flags.finding: Fixed dislocation with limited abduction in an infant older than 6 months
red_flags.meaning: Reduction is likely harder; needs pediatric orthopedic surgery and possible open reduction.

red_flags.finding: Abnormal neurologic exam such as spasticity, hypotonia, or asymmetric reflexes
red_flags.meaning: Secondary hip dysplasia from neuromuscular disease; needs neurology and orthopedics evaluation.

red_flags.finding: Painful limp in a walking-age child
red_flags.meaning: Consider older child DDH but also septic arthritis or transient synovitis; image promptly and do not assume benign until evaluated.

complications.name: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
clues: Occurs after treatment, especially with forceful or extreme positioning
Radiograph shows sclerosis, fragmentation, or collapse of the femoral head

complications.name: Residual acetabular dysplasia
clues: Radiographs show a shallow acetabulum after treatment

complications.name: Recurrent subluxation or dislocation
clues: Clicking or instability after harness or surgery
Radiograph or ultrasound shows lateralized femoral head
Asymmetric folds or leg length discrepancy returns

complications.name: Early-onset hip osteoarthritis
clues: Activity-related hip pain in adolescence or young adulthood
Radiograph shows joint space loss, osteophytes, residual acetabular dysplasia

special_populations.differences: Newborn exam may produce soft clicks or laxity that resolves. Ultrasound before 4-6 weeks can overcall physiologic immaturity; if risk factors or equivocal exam, repeat ultrasound at 4-6 weeks. Mild dysplasia often stabilizes without treatment.

After walking age, the diagnosis presents as a painless limp, waddling gait, leg length discrepancy, or lordosis rather than a positive Ortolani or Barlow maneuver. Radiographs are needed; closed or open reduction and pelvic or femoral osteotomy may be required.

key_questions.question: Was the baby born breech, and was there any oligohydramnios during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Breech presentation or oligohydramnios, both strong risk factors for DDH

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have a history of hip dysplasia or a dislocated hip as a baby?
key_questions.looking_for: First-degree relative with DDH, a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you noticed a clunk, click, or any asymmetry in the baby's hips or thighs?
key_questions.looking_for: A palpable clunk (not a soft click), asymmetric thigh or buttock creases, or one leg appearing shorter

key_questions.question: Does one leg seem harder to spread apart during diaper changes, or does the baby hold one leg differently?
key_questions.looking_for: Limited hip abduction or an externally rotated, shortened-appearing leg

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any fever, fussiness, or refusal to move one leg?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence of fever, pain, or irritability; these suggest septic arthritis rather than DDH

key_questions.question: Is the baby a girl, and is this her first pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Female sex and firstborn status, moderate risk factors

key_questions.question: For an older child: has there been any limp, waddling gait, or complaint of hip pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Painless limp or waddling gait in a walking-age child, suggestive of late-presenting DDH

key_questions.question: How are you swaddling the baby?
key_questions.looking_for: Tight swaddling with hips extended and adducted, a weak risk factor

reasoning_points: Positive Ortolani maneuver: a palpable clunk of the femoral head reducing into the acetabulum with abduction
Positive Barlow maneuver: the femoral head slips out of the acetabulum with adduction and posterior pressure
Risk factors present: female, firstborn, breech presentation, or family history of DDH
Asymmetric skin folds, limited hip abduction, or Galeazzi sign (one knee lower with hips flexed)
Ultrasound showing alpha angle less than 60 degrees or femoral head coverage less than 50% in an infant under 4-6 months
AP pelvis radiograph showing acetabular index greater than 30 degrees or femoral head lateral to Perkins line in an older infant
No fever, pain, or irritability, making septic arthritis unlikely
Appropriate referral to pediatric orthopedics for treatment

medium: 6-week-old infant with only limited hip abduction and a Galeazzi sign; no Ortolani or Barlow
Bilateral DDH causing symmetric folds and no leg length discrepancy
Infant with multiple risk factors but a normal screening exam, requiring ultrasound for confirmation
hard: 18-month-old child with painless limp and waddling gait; radiograph shows a dislocated hip but history lacks classic infant findings
Infant with fever and fussiness whose parents report a 'click'; must differentiate from septic arthritis
Older child with residual acetabular dysplasia presenting as hip pain, previously treated and now with recurrent subluxation
